A disease called consumption had already killed Mercy Brown's mother and older sister. That winter, it killed Mercy too, at just 19. Now her brother Edwin was seriously ill. episodes.script: A volcano helped create the monster behind del Toro's Frankenstein. In 1815, Mount Tambora exploded in what's now Indonesia. It was the largest eruption in recorded history. Its ash rose high, and the next year became the Year Without a Summer. Snow fell in parts of New York and Maine in June. Frost killed crops, and food riots broke out in Europe. In Switzerland, cold, stormy weather trapped a group of young writers indoors by Lake Geneva. And one of them, just 18 years old, was about to dream up a monster. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 2.

At Lord Byron's villa, the poet proposed they each write a ghost story. Mary Godwin, the future Mary Shelley, struggled at first. Then one night, she had what she later called a waking dream. She pictured a pale student kneeling beside a creature he had built. That vision became the seed of Frankenstein. But Byron's own doctor would turn the same challenge into a very different monster. episodes.script: That same ghost story challenge also helped create the modern vampire. In Part 2, Byron's challenge sparked the idea for Frankenstein. Its vampire was a charming aristocrat, a model that helped shape Dracula. But it was wrongly credited to Byron. And Frankenstein came out with no author's name at all. episodes.script: Before Spielberg's War of the Worlds, a radio version supposedly panicked America. The evidence tells a different story. The night before Halloween in 1938, Orson Welles aired his version on CBS radio. Dance music kept getting cut off by fake news bulletins. Reporters described a strange object landing in New Jersey. Anyone who tuned in late could wait almost 40 minutes to hear it was fiction. By morning, newspapers across the country were reporting mass panic. But a ratings survey that night found only a tiny share of homes were even listening. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 2.

episodes.series_title: The Martian Panic That Barely Happened
episodes.episode_title: The Ratings That Sank the Panic Story
episodes.youtube_title: The Martian Panic That Barely Happened (Part 2/3)
episodes.script: Almost no one surveyed that night was listening to the Martian invasion. In Part 1, newspapers claimed a Martian radio drama had panicked America. A ratings service surveyed 5,000 homes, and just 2 percent were listening to Welles. Yet within three weeks, newspapers ran at least 12,500 articles about the broadcast. Later, a Princeton study estimated over a million people were frightened. But it relied on audience numbers far higher than other surveys found. And being scared isn't the same as panicking. Meanwhile, newspapers were losing money to the very thing they blamed. Subscribe so you don't miss Part 3.
episodes.cliffhanger: Meanwhile, newspapers were losing money to the very thing they blamed.
episodes.description: Newspapers ran thousands of stories about a nationwide panic, but a survey from that night found almost nobody listening. Do you trust old headlines?

episodes.script: The great Martian panic story may have been about advertising money. In Part 2, a survey found only 2 percent of homes were listening to the broadcast. During the Great Depression, radio had been pulling advertising money away from newspapers. Two media scholars argue newspapers seized the chance to paint radio as irresponsible and unreliable. And many of the panic stories fell apart. No deaths or suicides linked to the show were ever verified. Some listeners truly were scared. The Martians landed on radio. The panic mostly landed in newspapers. Subscribe for a new true story every day.
